core_principles.text: Performing a partial lunge with anterolateral 45-degree resistance can be used to increase the VMO/VL muscle activity ratio.
Restoring the balance between the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) and vastus lateralis (VL) muscles is important for maintaining proper patellar alignment.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 22 healthy participants, the VMO/VL EMG activity ratio during a partial lunge with anterolateral 45-degree resistance was significantly higher than with no resistance and lateral 90-degree resistance (p < 0.05).
There was no significant difference in VMO, VL, and VMO/VL muscle activity between male and female subjects during the partial lunge exercises (p > 0.05).
The prevalence of patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is approximately 25% and is more common in women.

consequences.text: An imbalance between the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) and vastus lateralis (VL) muscles causes a lateral force deviation, increasing pressure on the patella and joint, which can lead to patellofemoral pain.

core_principles.text: Keep the upper body upright during the lunge to maintain proper alignment.
Position the ankle joint of the front foot at approximately 60 degrees of abduction to increase vastus medialis oblique (VMO) muscle activation.
Apply resistance from an anterolateral 45-degree direction to the knee during the lunge to selectively increase the VMO/VL muscle activation ratio.
For early-stage rehabilitation where high force is not desired, a partial lunge with approximately 50 degrees of knee flexion can be utilized.

common_mistakes.text: Leaning the torso forward during the lunge instead of keeping the upper body upright.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 21 healthy adults in their 20s, the VMO/VL EMG activity ratio was significantly higher during a partial lunge with 45-degree anterolateral resistance (125.31 ± 20.74 %MVIC) compared to no resistance (111.71 ± 21.59 %MVIC) and 90-degree lateral resistance (113.16 ± 24.75 %MVIC).
An ankle abduction angle of 60 degrees during the lunge was shown to maximize VMO muscle activation.
The partial lunge in this study was performed by lowering the body to a knee flexion angle of approximately 50 degrees.

VMO muscle activation reached 58.02 ± 19.71 %MVIC under 45-degree anterolateral resistance, compared to 47.75 ± 18.12 %MVIC with no resistance and 46.45 ± 16.83 %MVIC with 90-degree lateral resistance.

consequences.text: Failing to selectively activate the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) relative to the vastus lateralis (VL) can reduce knee joint stability and is associated with patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS).
